newsitem.title: USA: Stocks fall, dollar takes break from climb. [CORRECTED 01:30 GMT 11/4]
newsitem.headline: Stocks fall, dollar takes break from climb. [CORRECTED 01:30 GMT 11/4]

text.p: Wall Street stocks ended lower Thursday as investors took to the sidelines ahead of Friday's March wholesale price report, and the dollar fell from a 4-1/2 year high against the yen as U.S. and Japanese officials expressed concern about its strength.

The Dow Jones industrial average closed down 23.79 points at 6,540.05. In the broader market, declines led advances 1,307 to 1,092 on moderate volume of 421 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
Technology and financial stocks led the market lower for the second consecutive day. Analysts said the cautious atmosphere would likely put a cap on any near-term gains in stocks.
"The sentiment is pretty negative here," said Peter Green, director of technical research at Gruntal & Co. "If we do go higher, it's going to be met with selling."
The pessimism was evident in a report that showed new investment in mutual funds fell sharply last month.

According to the Investment Company Institute, a mutual fund trade group, new cash flowing to stock mutual funds slowed to an estimated $9.5 billion in March from the $18.45 billion inflow in February.
It said the March figure was the lowest since July, 1996, when the stock market endured a significant correction.
The Nasdaq Composite index, heavy with technology companies, lost 13.66 points to 1,235.77.

In the U.S. Treasury bond market, the benchmark 30-year bond slipped 3/32 of a point, or 93.75 cents per $1,000 face value, and its yield, which moves in the opposite direction of its price, edged up to 7.11 percent from 7.10 percent Wednesday.
The dollar fell from Wednesday's high after Japan's Finance Ministry and U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said they were concerned about the currency's rapid rise.

The dollar rallied early Thursday to 127.16 yen (corrects from 127.10 yen) in Tokyo, its highest level since August 1992, before Japanese government officials said the yen's recent declines were too rapid and excessive.
Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka was quoted as saying that recent yen moves were obviously excessive, which the market took as a warning that Japan would try to curb the dollar's rise.
The dollar also was knocked lower after Rubin said for the first time that the United States shared Japan's concern about the weak yen. The U.S. currency fell to 125.85 yen from 126.80 on Wednesday.
Rubin, who spoke on CNBC television, stressed that the United States had not abandoned its policy of advocating a strong dollar, which initially gave the dollar a brief lift.
"Our policy is absolutely unchanged," Rubin said in answer to a question about the dollar and possible confusion in financial markets about U.S. policy.
Against the mark, the dollar shook off supportive comments from German finance officials, and fell to 1.7190 marks from 1.7255 marks on Wednesday.
In other trading, the dollar fell to 1.4685 Swiss francs from 1.4788, and it rose to Canadian $1.3937 from C$1.3895.
The British pound rose to $1.6230 from $1.6200.
In commodites markets, grain and soybean prices rose amid strong exports and a final blast of wintry weather in the Midwest that prompted worries about crop damage, planting delays and flooding.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, corn for May delivery rose 4-3/4 cents a bushel to $3.03-3/4. May delivery wheat closed up 7-1/2 cents at $3.93 and May soybeans up 7-3/4 cents at $8.55-1/4.
Meteorologists said frigid temperatures that are expected to persist through the weekend could damage winter wheat from Kansas to Texas that is just emerging from dormancy at the start of spring.
In overseas stock trading, London's FTSE 100 index rose 20.9 points to 4,313.2. Tokyo's 225-share Nikkei average lost 217.62 points to 17,485.75.
